hints: `protected` and `private` don't hide properties at run time.

With a target of ES2022 or later, declared fields are created (as `undefined`) in declaration order before the constructor body assigns them. The parameter property is assigned after `super(...)` returns.
exercises.solution: All three are ordinary run-time properties; access modifiers are erased. The field declarations `sku` and `name` become class fields, created in that order when the `Product` part of the object is initialised; the constructor then assigns their values. The parameter property `coverPriceCents` is assigned in `Book`'s constructor after `super(name)`. Output: `[ 'sku', 'name', 'coverPriceCents' ]`.

hints: Getters live on the prototype, so they aren't own keys.
exercises.solution: `super.fahrenheit` computes 21.7 × 9 / 5 + 32 = 71.06, rounded to 71. `Reading` extends `Temperature`, so `instanceof` is true. The only own property is the parameter property `celsius`; the getter is on the prototype. Output: `71 true celsius`.

hints: Which of the two kinds of privacy exists at run time?
exercises.solution: TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time check, so `pin` is serialised like any other property. `#secret` is a JavaScript private field, invisible to `JSON.stringify` and `Object.keys`. Output: `{"pin":1234}`.

exercises.prompt: `Product` is an abstract class with `abstract priceCents(): number`. Which of these are compile errors? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `new Product("Atlas")`
options.feedback: Yes: `Cannot create an instance of an abstract class`.

options.label: `class Poster extends Product {}`
options.feedback: Yes: a concrete subclass must implement every abstract member (error TS2515).

options.label: `class Book extends Product { priceCents() { return 1500; } }`
options.feedback: Not yet. This is a correct concrete subclass.

options.label: `const items: Product[] = [];`
options.feedback: Not yet. An abstract class is a perfectly good type; only instantiating it directly is forbidden.

hints: Abstract classes can be used as types and extended; they can't be instantiated, and their abstract members must be filled in.
exercises.solution: (a) and (b) are errors. An abstract class can't be instantiated, and a non-abstract subclass must implement its abstract members. Using it as a type (d) and extending it properly (c) are exactly what it's for.

exercises.prompt: A Node project uses `"module": "nodenext"` and `"type": "module"`. In `main.ts`, how do you import `convert` from the source file `temperature.ts` in the same folder?

options.label: `import { convert } from "./temperature.js";`
options.feedback: Yes. You write the name of the file that exists at run time; TypeScript maps it to the `.ts` source.

options.label: `import { convert } from "./temperature";`
options.feedback: Not yet. Under nodenext this is error TS2835: relative imports need explicit file extensions, as Node itself requires.

options.label: `import { convert } from "./temperature.ts";`
options.feedback: Not yet. That works only with `allowImportingTsExtensions` (or `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`), typically when Node strips types itself.

options.label: `const { convert } = require("./temperature");`
options.feedback: Not yet. That's CommonJS; the project is an ES module project.

hints: Which file will Node actually load after compilation?
exercises.solution: Node loads `temperature.js`, the compiled file, and requires full file names in ES module imports. TypeScript follows the same rule under `nodenext`, so you write `./temperature.js` and the compiler resolves it to `temperature.ts` while checking.

exercises.prompt: You install a popular JavaScript package that ships no type declarations, and `import` it in TypeScript. What do professionals usually do first?

options.label: Install its community types from DefinitelyTyped, e.g. `npm install --save-dev @types/<name>`
options.feedback: Yes. Most popular untyped packages have an `@types` package; only if none exists do you write a small declaration yourself.

options.label: Turn off `strict` so the import is allowed
options.feedback: Not yet. That weakens checking for the whole project to work around one import.

options.label: Rewrite the package in TypeScript
options.feedback: Not yet. A declaration file is enough; the package's JavaScript is fine.

options.label: Cast every value from the package to `any`
options.feedback: Not yet. That spreads unchecked values through your code.

hints: Where do types for JavaScript packages that don't ship their own come from?
exercises.solution: The DefinitelyTyped project publishes types for thousands of JavaScript packages under the `@types` scope on npm. If none exist, write a minimal `declare module "name" { ... }` covering just what you use.

exercises.prompt: With `verbatimModuleSyntax` enabled, `import { Unit } from "./temperature.js";` (where `Unit` is a type alias) is an error. Why does the option insist on `import type`?

options.label: So that a tool removing types one file at a time knows the import can be deleted without looking at the other module
options.feedback: Yes. With the import marked as type-only, the JavaScript output is predictable, and fast type-stripping tools work correctly.

options.label: Because types cannot be exported from modules
options.feedback: Not yet. Types are exported and imported all the time; the question is only how the import is written.

options.label: Because `import type` is faster at run time
options.feedback: Not yet. Type-only imports produce no run-time code either way; the issue is knowing that when compiling one file in isolation.

options.label: Because `Unit` is a union type
options.feedback: Not yet. The same applies to any type: interfaces, aliases of every kind.

hints: Think about a tool like Node's type stripping, which sees only one file at a time.
exercises.solution: In `import { Unit } from ...`, nothing in `main.ts` itself says whether `Unit` is a type (to be erased) or a value (to be kept). A compiler that sees the whole program can find out; a per-file tool cannot. `verbatimModuleSyntax` therefore requires `import type { Unit }` (or `import { type Unit }`), so that every import's fate is visible locally.
